Others are outside of these service zones, and rely on wells, water kiosks, or hauling their water by truck or bicycle.

criterion_notes.c1: Discusses household and community drinking-water service access, specifically disconnection or retreat from centralized piped water systems and reliance on modular, adaptive, and decentralized (MAD) water provisioning (wells, water kiosks, water hauling, bottled water, filtration).
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the op-ed briefly references governance and regulatory context (municipal service zones, fear of building-code inspections in an abstract anecdote, municipal underbounding cited from prior literature, lack of water-quality regulation in decentralized systems, and informal community water oversight), but its central focus is proposing a normative ethical framework for applied anthropologists working on MAD water interventions rather than examining a governance factor. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it clearly fails (c2 = no) because rule-type mechanisms (such as building-code enforcement or municipal underbounding) are mentioned only in passing as background motivation or literature citations rather than examined as an exposure governing service access. Under both the plain and narrow readings of Criterion 2, the overall full-text decision remains exclude because the paper also lacks empirical evidence (Criterion 3).
criterion_notes.c3: Explicitly published as a 4-page Opinion Editorial ('OPINION EDITORIAL' on p. 2; 'this op ed' on p. 5) proposing a three-part ethical framework for applied anthropologists. Aside from a single uncontextualized conversational quote in the abstract and general references to the consortium's broader published research, it presents no empirical study design, sample, data collection or analysis methods, primary empirical findings, or systematic empirical synthesis -> exclude under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Conceptually discusses unmanaged and managed household withdrawal/disconnection from centralized water systems, affordability, and contamination risks, but reports no empirical access outcome data.
criterion_notes.c5: Because this is a non-empirical opinion editorial, there is no defined study sample, empirical exposure, measured outcome, or empirical study design.

country: United States (with general Global North and Global South discussion)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Full text is a 4-page Opinion Editorial ('OPINION EDITORIAL') in Human Organization proposing a normative ethical framework for applied anthropologists regarding household 'managed retreat' from centralized piped water systems toward modular, adaptive, and decentralized (MAD) water systems. Although it touches conceptually on household water service access and mentions regulatory/governance issues (service zones, building-code inspections, municipal underbounding) in passing, it reports no empirical study design, sample, methods, or primary empirical findings, nor is it a systematic empirical synthesis. It also fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type reading because its analytical focus is researcher ethics around socio-technical MAD interventions rather than a legal or administrative rule governing service access.
